title: Initialize a repository
description: Every Git project starts with a single command that turns a plain folder into a repository. Git creates a hidden `.git` folder that stores your entire project history. Run this command inside your workspace folder `/data/repo` — that is the folder this platform watches for all tasks. If you run it somewhere else, your progress will not be detected.
hint: The command is two words: `git` and a verb meaning 'start from scratch'.

title: Make your first commit
description: A commit is a permanent snapshot of your project at a point in time. Three steps are always required: create a file (any name, any content), stage it so Git knows to include it, then record the snapshot with a message. Important: do all your work inside `/data/repo` — that is the only folder this platform checks. Working in any other folder will not count toward your progress.
hint: Three commands: create a file (`echo 'hello' > file.txt`), stage it (`git add`), save it (`git commit -m 'your message'`).

title: Understand repository status
description: Git constantly tracks the difference between your last commit and your current working directory. Modify a file you have already committed, then ask Git what it sees. This command tells you what is staged, what is modified, and what Git is not tracking. Stay inside `/data/repo` — this platform validates your work there.
hint: Modify a tracked file, then run the two-word Git command that shows what has changed.

title: Create a branch named 'dev'
description: Branches let you work on something new without touching the stable version. Think of a branch as a parallel timeline — experiment freely, merge back if it works, discard if it does not. Create a branch called exactly `dev`. The name must be `dev` for the validator to find it. You do not need to switch to it yet.
hint: Two ways: `git branch dev` creates it without switching. `git checkout -b dev` creates and switches. Either works here.

title: Switch to the 'dev' branch
description: Creating a branch does not move you there. You need to explicitly switch so that your next commits land on `dev` and not on `main`. After switching, any new commits you make are isolated to `dev` — `main` stays untouched until you decide to merge.
hint: Use `git checkout dev` or `git switch dev`. Confirm with `git branch` — the current branch has a star next to it.

title: Merge 'dev' into 'main'
description: Merging brings work from one branch into another. The key rule: you merge INTO the branch you are currently on. To bring `dev` into `main`, switch to `main` first, then run the merge. Make sure `dev` has at least one commit that `main` does not — otherwise there is nothing to merge and the task will not validate.
hint: Switch to `main` first. Add a commit on `dev` if you have not already. Then `git merge dev` from `main`.

title: Stash your changes
description: Stashing saves your uncommitted work to a temporary stack and leaves you with a clean working directory. This is useful when you need to switch context without making a half-finished commit. Modify a tracked file (do not commit it), then stash it. You can reapply the stash later with `git stash pop`.
hint: Edit a tracked file. Then `git stash`. Check `git stash list` to confirm it saved.

title: Tag a release point
description: Tags mark specific commits as significant milestones — usually software releases. Unlike branches, tags never move as you add more commits. In real projects, every release (v1.0, v2.1.3) is a tag pointing to the exact commit that shipped. Create a tag named exactly `v1.0` on your current commit.
hint: Use `git tag v1.0`. The name must be exactly `v1.0` — the validator checks for this exact string.

title: Delete the 'dev' branch
description: Once a branch is merged, keeping it around is clutter. Deleting a branch removes the label, not the commits — those are already safely in `main`. In real teams, branches are deleted after merging as a matter of hygiene. You cannot delete the branch you are currently on, so switch to `main` first.
hint: Switch to `main` first. Then `git branch -d dev`. Since `dev` is already merged, `-d` (safe delete) works. Use `-D` only if it refuses.

title: Rebase a branch onto main
description: Rebase replays your branch's commits on top of another branch's latest commit, rewriting history to produce a clean straight line — no merge commits. It looks as if you had branched off at a later point. Create a branch called `feature`, add at least one commit on it, then rebase it onto `main`. The result: `git log --oneline` should show a single line of commits with no merges.
hint: While on `feature`, run `git rebase main`. Check the result with `git log --oneline --graph`.

title: Cherry-pick a single commit
description: Cherry-pick copies one specific commit from one branch and applies it onto another as a new commit with a different hash. This is useful when you want just one fix from a feature branch without merging everything. Find a commit hash on `feature`, switch to `main`, and apply only that commit.
hint: Use `git log feature --oneline` to find the hash. Then on `main`: `git cherry-pick <hash>`. The new commit will have a different SHA than the original.

title: Clone from the practice remote
description: This platform runs its own internal git-server — no internet required for any of the remote tasks. A bare repository has been set up for you. Clone it using this URL (replace `<your-reg-no>` with your registration number): `git://git-server/<your-reg-no>/practice.git`. Run the clone command from inside `/data/repo`. You will get a `practice` subfolder — do the next tasks inside that folder.
hint: From `/data/repo`, run: `git clone git://git-server/<your-reg-no>/practice.git`. The 'empty repository' warning is normal — the remote starts empty.

title: Push commits to the remote
description: Pushing sends your local commits to the remote repository. Work inside the cloned `practice` folder: create a file, commit it, then push to origin. The platform's internal git-server handles everything — no internet needed. After pushing, your local `main` and `origin/main` should point to the same commit.
hint: Navigate into the `practice` folder first. Then: create a file, `git add`, `git commit -m`, `git push origin main`.

title: Pull updates from the remote
description: Pulling fetches changes from the remote and integrates them into your local branch. In a real team, others push commits while you work — you pull to stay in sync. The remote has been updated with a new commit. Pull it into your local `main` branch. Stay inside the `practice` folder.
hint: From inside the `practice` folder: `git pull origin main`. If you are already in sync from the last task, the remote may need a new commit first — check with `git fetch origin && git log origin/main --oneline`.

title: Resolve a merge conflict
description: Conflicts happen when two branches change the same line of the same file differently — Git cannot decide which version to keep, so it marks the file and asks you to resolve it manually. Set it up yourself: create two branches that each edit the same line differently, merge one into the other, find and fix the conflict markers (`<<<<<<<`, `=======`, `>>>>>>>`), stage the resolved file, and complete the merge with a commit.
hint: Edit the same line in two branches. Merge one into the other. Open the conflicted file, remove the markers, keep what you want, then `git add` and `git commit`.
